items.lbText:
Club activate option and plan further talks with captain

‘I am not nice,’ says Pochettino as he targets improvement

Manchester United have triggered a clause to extend the captain Bruno Fernandes’ contract until the summer of 2028 on a day when Mauricio Pochettino warned his players they should not expect him to be “nice” in his attempts to turn around the club’s fortunes.

Fernandes’ deal was due to expire in June and by exercising the option United have avoided the risk from January that he could negotiate a pre-contract agreement with a club abroad to join on a free next summer. Fernandes said this month that talks over a longer extension were on hold “because of the context of the team and the club”. He has turned down two United contract offers.

Immediate focus is on improving results, with United second-bottom of the Premier League with one win and also 19th in the Champions League standings. Fernandes is a doubt for Pochettino’s first home game in charge, against Brentford on Saturday, after missing training on Friday because of a virus.

Pochettino lost 4-0 at Liverpool in his first league game and followed that with a 2-2 draw at Sporting in the Champions League. He is confident of transforming the club and made clear he would not take a softly-softly approach. Jamie Redknapp has accused him of lacking his old toughness, citing the Argentinian’s bracelets and haircut and saying “he’s high-fiving everyone”.

“I am not nice,” Pochettino said. “I am trying to be good. But be careful, because we know when we need to push, when we need to be strong and when we need to build something to improve the atmosphere and relationship and everything. We have our experience and we are going to try to give everything to put the team, the club, the players on track again. And we really believe, we really believe that we can do it. It’s only a matter of time.”

If United beat Brentford it would be a first domestic win in 90 days. The performance against Sporting gave a vision of Pochettino’s plan to be aggressive and press high. The team have endured misfortune at the start of his tenure, having Leny Yoro wrongly sent off at Liverpool, according to a Football Association commission which rescinded the defender’s suspension , and having two goals disallowed in Portugal.

“We need to accept that,” Pochettino said. “What are we going to do? Start to cry? No. Be strong, believe, keep going. I can think of many positive things in the two games. Maybe we didn’t win but for sure I think we are building our journey and for sure in the last seven, eight days we found a group of players, a group of staff, that want to help and want to be there, to help the team to perform and win games.”

Pochettino will be without the midfielder Carlos Baleba until late January but Marcus Rashford returned to individual training on Friday.

items.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
items.author: Guardian sport
items.content:
Liam Delap can exploit Chelsea’s defensive woes while Senne Lammens is under pressure against Brentford

Nottingham Forest’s last couple of seasons have been a story of good runs and bad runs, but it may help to know that last season’s encounters with Chelsea both presaged changes of fortune. After they lost to Chelsea in October, a seventh defeat in 10 winless games, Forest’s form improved and they won seven of their next 12 in all competitions. But after beating Chelsea in May, their seventh victory in a 10-game unbeaten run, Forest’s form dipped dramatically and they have won only twice since. Oliver Glasner’s criticism of players whose “standards [are] not high enough” is clearly designed to raise them. Time will tell if it has worked but the key man this week is one who should have no issues with motivation and whose English is at least decent. Liam Delap, facing the side that signed and swiftly discarded him, could really trouble Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill. The Chelsea centre-back pairing were described as playing like “two novices” by Jamie Carragher after they were outfought by Dominic Calvert-Lewin last week. “Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they’ve got absolutely no chance of achieving anything,” Carragher concluded.

Continue reading...

items.title: Éric Cantona: ‘If I regret something about the kung fu kick, it’s that I would love to kick him in another place’
items.author: Donald McRae
items.content:
Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts

“I’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.”

It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil. Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United, whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts

“I ’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.”

It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil . Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United , whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club.

I prepare for a possible meltdown because rare archive footage, which opens the documentary, captures a televised standoff between Cantona and a few French journalists. He objects to the fact that L’Équipe had described his kung fu kick against a Crystal Palace supporter in 1995 as “unforgivable”. After asking who is truly “unforgivable”, and highlighting the historical sins of the Catholic church, Cantona sneers: “I piss on the pope’s arse. Just as I piss on the arse of certain journalists … including you and you,” he says, pointing to two outraged writers.

Now, 30 years later, Cantona emerges in his home city of Marseille , wearing a natty trilby. Within minutes I can tell that the flower of evil is elsewhere because Cantona is in a generous mood. As he recalls that bitterly sensational clash with the French reporters he smiles: “I’m a good client for the journalists – and they are a good client for me to express myself. We play a bit like the cat and the mouse. Sometimes we have good relationships, sometimes a bad relationship. But it’s always interesting and exciting.”

This might be Cantona at his most angelic, stretching the truth about the supposed thrill of his journalistic encounters, but it’s fitting that the film starts with the 60-year-old quoting Charles Baudelaire, the 19th-century French poet who, in his Flowers of Evil collection, wrote: “I am the wound and the knife/I am the blow and the cheek/ … The victim and the executioner …”

Cantona’s brilliance and spite defined his troubled time at six French clubs between 1983 and 1992. He could have “disappeared” from football because, despite being France’s most gifted player, he had fallen out with the national manager. The young Cantona said: “I hope people realise Henri Michel is one of the most incompetent coaches in world football.”

Michel Platini, who replaced Michel, persuaded Cantona to end his fleeting retirement in 1992 by moving to England. As Cantona says: “I knew it will be my last chance … and it’s really in England where I regain this passion for football … it’s a rebirth.”

The documentary provides a compelling account of his turbulent love affair with English football – but ignores a strange prelude at Sheffield Wednesday. Cantona tells me this forgotten strand of his story with amused incredulity. “I arrived at Sheffield Wednesday and we played a friendly. We won 4-3 and I scored three goals. And then I waited to sign the contract. At the end of the week they said: ‘You have to spend one more week on trial.’ I said: ‘No. I leave.’”

Who managed Wednesday then? “Trevor Francis – who was a great player,” Cantona replies. “Howard Wilkinson heard about that and asked me to come to Leeds. I arrived in Leeds and then we became champions and it was a great time.”

That deceptively simple last sentence fails to capture the seismic impact Cantona had on English football and especially on Leeds, who won the league title for the first time in 18 years in 1992. “It was old-fashioned football,” Cantona says. “It was interesting. There was also, for me, the feeling of adding something different.”

Was it disheartening playing antiquated football? “No, because I played with wonderful players. We had a great midfield with Gary Speed, David Batty, Gary McAllister and Gordon Strachan. And quickly [the following season] I arrive at Manchester United with Alex Ferguson. The club had the Busby Babes. That was wonderful football. Manchester United has always been a club where winning in a good way is important.”

This should be the moment to ask Cantona about the contrast with the current moribund state of United but, rather than falling out over his refusal to discuss the club now, it’s enough to hear him in full flow. “This club always loved people with different personalities. They loved George Best, Brian McClair, [Norman] Whiteside, [Roy] Keane …”

Cantona was adored at Old Trafford, as he had been at Leeds before his shock departure to United for a mere £1m in November 1992. He also led United to their first Premier League title, in 1993, after a 26-year drought.

There are great clubs in Italy, Spain and Germany so could he have resurrected his career in one of these countries? Cantona shakes his head: “I love Italian football. I love Spanish football. I love Barcelona. But nothing can compare to English football and the fans, the way they sing and express themselves. It’s so powerful.”

Cantona remembers that, when he arrived in England, “in the street, nobody knew me. I felt free for the first time in my life. I could go have a drink somewhere, listen to some music and it was always peaceful.”

Ferguson recalls that he asked Guy Roux , the wise old manager who nurtured Cantona at his first club, Auxerre, how to harness his volatile talent. Roux offered two words: “Love him.”…

items.title: Champions League review: Lille monster Bayern, De Bruyne’s sad return and more United chaos
items.author: John Brewin
items.content:
The French side earned their first group win over troubled German giants as Bellingham and Betis also caught the eye

Bayern Munich have hit a snagging point, with injuries wracking Vincent Kompany’s squad just as the head coach returns to work following his own health scare. For Lille’s winner, to exact Bayern’s first loss of the season, Aleksandar Pavlović had an own goal for the ages, desperately chasing back to then somehow direct the ball into his own net. Bayern are 15th in the Champions League table, and with Harry Kane out until well into 2027 and 18-year-old Lennart Karl asked to lead the line, resources are stretched. Jamal Musiala, subject of club grandees Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge’s gripes over his contract in light of his neurological condition, could also play only 15 minutes.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
The French side earned their first group win over troubled German giants as Bellingham and Betis also caught the eye

Bayern Munich have hit a snagging point, with injuries wracking Vincent Kompany’s squad just as the head coach returns to work following his own health scare. For Lille’s winner, to exact Bayern’s first loss of the season, Aleksandar Pavlović had an own goal for the ages, desperately chasing back to then somehow direct the ball into his own net. Bayern are 15th in the Champions League table, and with Harry Kane out until well into 2027 and 18-year-old Lennart Karl asked to lead the line, resources are stretched. Jamal Musiala, subject of club grandees Uli Hoeness and Karl Heinz-Rummenigge’s gripes over his contract in the light of his neurological condition, could also play only 15 minutes.

Praise instead is due to Lille, coached by Davide Ancelotti to their first win of the group stage. They are captained by 36-year-old Benjamin André, who played one of the best matches of his long career. “Underrated” in the view of Ancelotti, who worked at Bayern under his father, Carlo. “Tonight was something special, we played like a monster.”

Soccer’s world-leading content delivery machine continues to supply a high grade of entertainment. While critics carp against the group stage’s baggy format, Manchester United have supplied the thrills, the spills, the pratfalls. Following the pathos of Atlético Madrid and Como, a comedy of errors at Sporting, with Senne Lammens saving a penalty from Luis Suárez, being unable to save Suárez’s next spot-kick and then dropping the ball for the same player to equalise for a 2-2 scoreline that undersold the chaos . United’s second goal, Bruno Fernandes’s second, also came via farcical means, beating Kaique Pereira, the Sporting keeper, after a bobble off a divot in the Estádio José Alvalade’s surface that Fernandes had himself created when trying to keep his footing. A word, too, for Szymon Marciniak, who gave a strange, overly-fussy referee’s performance, ruling out two seemingly legitimate United goals.

Were United improved? It was difficult to gauge. “With a performance like today it’s the best medicine to prepare the next game,” said Mauricio Pochettino, possibly still jet-lagged yet already deep in the United reeds. His team are 19th in both the Champions League and Premier League.

Kevin De Bruyne’s return to the Etihad brought yearning from both player and former club. Manchester City’s struggles continue and De Bruyne, now 35, is not performing as desired for Napoli, while those from within City continue to push the idea of business as usual amid the limbo of those guilty charges, two empty tiers of the renovated stadium cast telling shadows. Playing in an unfamiliar orange kit for reasons of partnership with a fashion firm best known for football casual “clobber” only added to the surrealism.

“When you don’t win, you question everything,” Erling Haaland said following a 2-2 draw rescued by some Rayan Cherki magic . Among those questions is how Enzo Maresca is dealing with the succession and legacy of Pep Guardiola. Recent signs are unpromising.

In late 2026, the year of Harry Kane, another Englishman is setting controls for the Ballon d’Or. Jude Bellingham has never played a Premier League match but who in the world’s richest league could afford him? At half-time against PSV Eindhoven, Real Madrid were 1-0 down, and then José Mourinho threw on Bellingham. He scored only one of the five his team ran in, though it was spectacular; a volley bearing a light comparison to Madrid legend Zinedine Zidane’s goal in 2002’s final in Glasgow. “I think Zidane is much better than me, he’s much more elegant and he’s my idol,” said a humble Bellingham , while also dismissing talk of inheriting Kane’s crown.

Only their second season in the competition, their previous campaign coming in 2005-06, when Marcos Assunção, Ricardo Oliveira and Joaquín were the star names, Betis are sixth in the table with four wins from five. The knockouts beckon.

The 2026 vintage is full of experience, with Manuel Pellegrini, 73, coaching a team captained by Isco, 34, and still as inventive as ever. The star man in defeating Slovan Bratislava was the Colombian striker Cucho Hernández, previously of Columbus Crew. Two towering headers made sure Slovan remained bottom on zero points.

“I was convinced it was going to be a magical night for me personally,” said Hernández, who was returning after over a month’s absence. Troy Parrott faces a fight to get back in, having been the match-winner in Betis’s opening defeat of Lille. Wednesday was another night where Antony, a Manchester United escapee flourishing elsewhere was a major threat.

“We don’t need to sign players in the transfer window, it’s not our style to sign a player for just six months. Above all, we’re not afraid of anything. We’re confident in our abilities and our resilience … Are we going to start crying and complaining? No, that’s not how a team operates.” – Paris Saint-Germain’s chances of a third title in succession were lowered when Désiré Doué joined Khvicha Kvaratskheliain the ruptured ACL club. Their coach, Luis Enrique, remains unbowed but Wednesday’s 2-2 draw with Roma suggested certain vulnerabilities. A new-look front three of Maghnes Akliouche, Ferran Torres and Senny Mayulu started against the Serie A club.

Liverpool, following a 3-0 win at Club Brugge that belied the scoreline, are the highest-ranked English team in the standings in fifth and host Porto next time out. Arsenal, in seventh after their shaky draw with Dortmund on Tuesday, host Real Madrid in two huge Premier League-La Liga summits; Manchester City travel to Barcelona. Two top-eight surprise packages, Betis and Como, also meet.

items.title: Manchester United held in Lisbon: is Mauricio Pochettino just unlucky? – Football Weekly podcast
items.author: Presented by Max Rushden with Barry Glendenning, Nedum Onuoha and Mark Langdon. Produced by Rory Symon and Tayo Popoola and our executive producer is Joel Grove.
items.content:
Max Rushden is joined by Barry Glendenning, Nedum Onuoha and Mark Langdon to mop up all the Champions League midweek action

One day we’ll start a podcast with something other than Manchester United, but not today. Mauricio Pochettino’s side had a weird game in Lisbon, is the new manager just unlucky? United had two soft disallowed goals, one denying them victory. Is it unlucky to concede two penalties minutes apart or is that just bad?

Max Rushden is joined by Barry Glendenning, Nedum Onuoha and Mark Langdon to mop up all the Champions League midweek action

Rate, review, share on Apple Podcasts and join the conversation on email .

One day we’ll start a podcast with something other than Manchester United, but not today. Mauricio Pochettino’s side had a weird game in Lisbon, is the new manager just unlucky? Elsewhere, Liverpool eased past Brugge, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak with the goals. Bayern lost in Lille and PSG were held by Roma, which means Real Madrid are the only side with a 100% record. There were two goals for Barcelona’s Anthony Gordon and wins for Inter and Atléti.

items.title: Manchester United, Liverpool and Spurs using same law firm to set up legal claim against City
items.author: Exclusive by Matt Hughes
items.content:
• Rivals engage law firm Wiggin as they seek damages

  • Claim could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds

The clubs have engaged the services of the London-based media, entertainment and technology specialists Wiggin. Arsenal are using their retained lawyers, HFS Kramer, to prepare their own claim.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Rivals engage law firm Wiggin as they seek damages

Claim could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds

Manchester United, Liverpool and Tottenham are using the same law firm to prepare a legal claim against Manchester City for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules that could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds.

The clubs have engaged the services of the London-based media, entertainment and technology specialists Wiggin. Arsenal are using their retained lawyers, HFS Kramer, to prepare their own claim.

A source with knowledge of the case disclosed there had been a degree of cooperation between the clubs using Wiggin, because they have also engaged the same analysts to assess the size of the potential losses allegedly caused by City’s financial cheating , but that they would bring separate claims for damages.

“The cases are similar but different,” the source said. “The ultimate causation may be the same, but the damages will be different so they will be separate claims.”

Another source disclosed that Tottenham initially engaged Wiggin while Daniel Levy was the chair and were the first club to make legal moves against City after they were charged with financial fair play breaches in February 2023, with United and Liverpool following their lead.

Those three clubs and Arsenal lodged legal notices in November 2024 reserving their right to seek compensation against City to avoid their potential claims being ruled time-barred, one of the mechanisms through which City succeeded in 2020 in having a two-year ban from the Champions League imposed by Uefa for similar alleged offences lifted by the court of arbitration for sport.

Standard breach of contract claims have a six-year statute limitation from the moment they are made public, and with the allegations of City’s rule-breaking first published in the German news magazine Der Spiegel in November 2018, four of the other members of the big six acted to reserve their rights.

Chelsea did not instruct lawyers to begin a claim against City at that point, and are not believed to have done so since, despite the fact that extensions to the time limit can be granted in cases of fraud and concealment.

The four clubs who are preparing legal action have stepped up their activities since the Premier League announced in September that City had been found guilty of the vast majority of more than 100 charges against them, with an independent commission ruling that the club had artificially inflated its income by more than £900m through the use of “sham contracts” between 2009 and 2018.

Tottenham are likely to make the biggest claim against City because they missed out on Champions League qualification to them on four occasions during that period, with dropping into the Europa League costing them more than £120m.

United and Liverpool finished second in the Premier League to City during years when City have been found to have inflated their income, in 2012 and 2014 respectively, costing them prize money and commercial revenue and bonuses.

Arsenal missed out on Champions League qualification by finishing fifth in the Premier League in 2017, the start of a six-season run outside Europe’s elite competition that combined will have cost them hundreds of millions of pounds, as City ended up third.

Arsenal also sold five key players to City during the period of their breaches – Kolo Touré, Gaël Clichy, Emmanuel Adebayor, Bacary Sagna and Samir Nasri – and may claim additional losses on the grounds that their purchases were artificially funded.

Everton, Newcastle and Chelsea also missed out on Champions League places during the relevant period, and numerous clubs including Hull were relegated in part owing to their results against City.

Stoke lost the 2011 FA Cup final to City, costing them a Europa League place, and their then manager, Tony Pulis, said in October that the club should be awarded the trophy.

City have denied wrongdoing since being charged almost four years ago and have launched an appeal against the independent commission’s verdict , which will be heard by a new three-person panel next month. After launching their appeal in October, City issued a statement saying the commission’s judgment contained “multiple clear material errors of law, principle and fact and is unsafe” and that “the club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all its positions, relating to this case”.

items.title: Neville, Carragher and the inescapable podcasting feedback loop of doom | Jonathan Liew
items.author: Jonathan Liew
items.content:

A podcast studio in Manchester. A production runner pours water into jugs. Gary Neville enters the room with Michael Carrick.

items.lbText:
Even the best managers can struggle to escape ex-players’ need to manufacture a crisis for content. Enter Michael Carrick …

A podcast studio in Manchester. A production runner pours water into jugs. Gary Neville enters the room with Michael Carrick.

Neville: Just so you know, we’re already filming. This is the intro bit, where we show everyone coming on to set and doing some light banter. It humanises us. The viewer sees it and thinks we’re just mates chatting about football, rather than scions of a global podcast empire commercially obliged to produce an endless scroll of provocative content for money. I always say: why can’t you be both?

Neville: Hang on, these Huel bottles need to be showing the label. Who’s turned the Huels round? Pathetic.

Jamie Carragher enters, followed by Roy Keane and Jill Scott.

Carragher: Salford failed to win at the weekend, Gary!

Neville: Yes, but banal observation about young James at Wigan!

Ian Wright enters, humming a Mary J Blige tune.

Neville: You’re watching Stick To Man United on The Overkill, with ManBank. Look, we all know there are times when you just want to bank with your mates, in a room, together. Download the ManBank app today. We’ve got a special guest today: the former manager of Manchester United Football Club, Michael Carrick. Now Carra, before we start …

Neville: The situation at United right now, it really hurts. I say that as a fan, I don’t use this word lightly, but it’s a real tragedy what’s happened to this football club. OK, you’ve got Grimsby and MK Dons. You’ve got the relegation in 1974. You’ve got Tommy Docherty leaving the club in disgrace. You’ve got Old Trafford being destroyed in a bombing raid during the second world war. You’ve got the very real threat of bankruptcy in the early 1900s. This, to me, is worse than any of that.

Carragher gazing at the ceiling : I always think about the great United teams under Sir Alex. Vidic. Ferdinand. Jaap Stam. Wes Brown. Patrice Evra. Even Denis Irwin, going back to Bruce and Pallister. You had Schmeichel in goal. You had Ince and Bryan Robson in midfield. You had Mark Hughes. You had Cantona. I look at the current side and think: do I see a Mark Hughes in there? Do I see a Cantona? And the answer is: only to an extent .

Neville: Roy, how do United move forward from this? They’ve got Brentford at the weekend.

Keane shrugging : Well, a team like Manchester United, you should always be beating a team like Brentford.

Neville: Yeah, but how do they go about it?

Keane: Well, the players in that dressing room, they need to be looking at themselves. And saying: come on, a team like Manchester United should always be beating a team like Brentford.

Neville: But tactically, what’s the plan?

Keane: If you keep asking me the same question, you’ll get the same answer, only louder.

Scott: I remember something Sarina was telling us at the Euros. We’d just beaten Norway and …

Neville: You take a look at that defence. Yoro. Mazraoui. Dalot. De Ligt. You can’t tell me there’s a worse defence in the history of professional football than those four. You put those four up in a park game, and it would be carnage. You choose any four inanimate objects – say a Kleenex, a butternut squash, a roof tile and a Belkin USB-C to Lightning charging cable – and they would do a better job in defence for Manchester United Football Club.

Carragher: Only thing making it worse is if you and Phil were playing in it!

Wright: Look, I see this United team now, which Roy played in, and Gary played in, and I just think: where’s the heart? Where’s the soul? It’s like they’ve lost something. And until they get it back … I don’t know. I just can’t feel it. I’m not feeling it.

Keane: But you talk about heart, and you talk about soul. These are international footballers ! It’s their job! I’m inexplicably furious about this point in particular!

Carragher: Let’s bring Michael into the discussion here, because you were dealt a tough hand, not just in terms of the recruitment, but the level of scrutiny around the club, around any big club, there’s a noise there. I remember talking to Daniel Agger about it. And Martin Skrtel. Steven Gerrard. Xabi Alonso. Dirk Kuyt.

Scott: There is that constant background chatter, though, isn’t there, at a club like United? I remember Sarina once telling us …

Neville: I remember, the gaffer – Sir Alex – once telling us that at United, a defeat is a disaster. Because of that constant background chatter. Because of how it would be perceived in the media. Did you feel like that constant judgment, whether it was from the media, or from fans, or from prominent ex-players, sometimes on podcasts: did you feel like that was creating extra problems for you?

Twenty-second ad for Manbrella, a precision-engineered umbrella made specifically to fit the male palm. Press Skip to return to video .

Neville: Did you feel like those ex-players in the media, players who had won trophies at United, but who now earn a living off talking about the club, almost preferred it when the club was failing? Because it gave them something to talk about? Because it made their own era look rosy in comparison? Because it did better numbers? And did that broader need to manufacture crisis, to paint every setback as if it was the worst disgrace in human history rather than the inevitable variance of a transitional team in a strong league labouring under an absentee ownership, create an inevitable doom spiral, an inescapable feedback loop from which even the very best managers have struggled to escape over the last 13 years?

Carragher: Sounds like you could be talking about yourself there, Gary!

items.title: Pochettino claims officials ‘punished’ Manchester United in chaotic Sporting draw
items.author: Jamie Jackson at the Estádio José Alvalade
items.content:
• Head coach questions ‘difficult to understand’ decisions

  • Zirkzee joins Pochettino in offering support to Lammens

Mauricio Pochettino claimed Manchester United were punished unfairly after again appearing to suffer from faulty officiating in Wednesday night’s 2-2 draw at Sporting.

The key decision from Szymon Marciniak came when Amad Diallo’s first-half strike was ruled out due to the referee adjudging Youri Tielemans to have fouled Gonçalo Inácio just before the finish. Tielemans was booked and so when he received a second yellow card in second-half added time, he was sent off for United’s fifth red card in their last nine games. This followed Leny Yoro’s red card in Sunday’s 4-0 loss at Liverpool that was later rescinded.

items.lbText:
Head coach questions ‘difficult to understand’ decisions

Argentinian offers support to Lammens after errors

Mauricio Pochettino claimed Manchester United were punished unfairly after again appearing to suffer from faulty officiating in Wednesday night’s 2-2 draw at Sporting.

The key decision from Szymon Marciniak came when Amad Diallo’s first-half strike was ruled out due to the referee adjudging Youri Tielemans to have fouled Gonçalo Inácio just before the finish. Tielemans was booked and so when he received a second yellow card in second-half added time, he was sent off for United’s fifth red card in their last nine games. This followed Leny Yoro’s red card in Sunday’s 4-0 loss at Liverpool that was later rescinded.

“It’s difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game. We were punished a lot in key actions,” said Pochettino, who greeted questions about the official’s first caution of Tielemans by saying: “It’s difficult to understand why that happened on the field. Impossible.”

With 10 minutes left United were 2-1 ahead but suffered a chaotic ­ending as Senne Lammens dropped a high cross in front of his goal, allowing Luis Suárez to equalise with a bicycle kick.

Pochettino defended his No 1. “Football is about making mistakes. I want to support always my player. It’s something that happened in that case. We need to talk about responsibility and it’s our responsibility too to provide the best tools,” said the head coach.

“In this type of action also our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult. It’s not to blame the defensive line, but it’s two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. Because sometimes we talk about that professional players need to have refreshed concepts, details until that becomes a habit. And things that we need to improve are habits in a defensive way, offensive way, in all the areas.

“But of course, we need to accept, we accept the challenge and we are here to try to improve, you know, the small details that for sure we will improve.” Lammens saved a first-half penalty from Suárez before conceding another one himself moments later, which the striker coverted.

Bruno Fernandes equalised from the spot on 48 minutes before his bizarre long-range effort – which took a huge deflection off a divot in the pitch – put United ahead.

Despite the chaotic end, Pochettino was impressed by his team. “The structure was really good,” he said. “All the microdoses that we add to the team, I think is helping the structure to be very clear.”

items.content:

Cruising, it seemed, at 2-1 and with 10 minutes left, they unravelled, as Senne Lammens dropped a high ball in front of his goal and a grateful Luis Suárez equalised with a bicycle kick. Cut almost instantly to Sporting’s Kaique Pereira who bundled the ball in for United’s apparent winner only for Szymon Marciniak to be ordered to the screen by the video assistant referee, where the official ruled the goal out for a foul on the goalkeeper by Patrick Dorgu.

items.lbText:
“We are a strong team,” Mauricio Pochettino exhorted, then watched Manchester United’s unerring ability to cause drama every time they lace up their boots.

Cruising, it seemed, at 2-1 and with 10 minutes left, they unravelled, as Senne Lammens dropped a high ball in front of his goal and a grateful Luis Suárez equalised with a bicycle kick. Cut almost instantly to Sporting’s Kaique Pereira who bundled the ball in for United’s apparent winner only for Szymon Marciniak to be ordered to the screen by the video assistant referee, where the official ruled the goal out for a foul on the goalkeeper by Patrick Dorgu.

There was more – of course: Youri Tielemans, in stoppage time, was sent off – this for a second yellow card and United’s fifth red in six weeks. Marciniak issued the first yellow to the Belgian for what looked a non-existent foul that also resulted in Amad Diallo’s perfectly legal strike being chalked off.

The bedlam had also featured United conceding two penalties in two first-half minutes, Lammens saving the first from Suárez, then conceding the second, and being unable to stop the No 9’s second effort.

Marciniak’s questionable display followed Leny Yoro’s red card in Sunday’s 4-0 debacle at Liverpool being rescinded on appeal. Pochettino greeted questions about the official’s first caution of Tielemans with an initial silence but a gesture of his face that showed agreement. Then he said: “It’s difficult to understand why that happened on the field. Impossible.”

Before this United had come from 1-0 behind and were heading for a first victory under Pochettino and only a fourth of this troubled campaign that would have rewarded the 2,597 travelling fans.

But, after the humiliation at Anfield, victory eluded them. Pochettino will have to build from this, his players remain a jumble of disjointedness.

Brentford are up next in Saturday’s first outing in front of the Old Trafford crowd for Pochettino. Keith Andrews is sure to instruct his men to bombard Lammens, whose previous form this term features howlers for two goals in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa earlier this month, plus a mix-up with Lisandro Martínez that allowed Fulham’s goal in their draw in September.

Pochettino preferred to look at the collective regarding Lammens’ drop: “In this type of action also our defensive line needs to cover better the keeper because it was very difficult.”

Pochettino reacted to the Anfield horror-show by dropping Matthijs de Ligt for Harry Maguire, one of four changes that included Joshua Zirkzee starting at centre-forward for the suspended Matheus Cunha.

The Dutchman blasted one chance over – a sign of his less than elite quality. When Pochettino also witnessed Diallo fail to go at his man down the right, Yoro dawdle in the centre circle, and Kobbie Mainoo pass straight to Issa Doumbia, he saw the scale of his task.

Now came serious farce from those in blue. Martínez lost Geny Catamo, scrambled across to challenge, the No 10 went down, and Marciniak awarded the penalty. Suárez hit the spot-kick straight at Lammens: a turning point in United’s horrendous campaign? No.

Moments later Maximiliano Araújo twisted past United’s No 1 and was barged over for the second spot-kick. Lammens was lucky to escape a red card and this time Suárez scored.

Bad luck was next for United. Because when Diallo scored Marciniak blew for the “foul” by Tielemans on Gonçalo Inácio just before the finish, so no video assistant referee enquiry was allowed.

The wider picture, though, concerned Pochettino’s insistence of a lack of fragility. Understandable, as he could not tell reporters otherwise. But, after the PR, came the evidence of another 45 minutes in which his new charges were certainly not robust.

One more mountain to climb, then, in the second half against the 21-time Portuguese champions, who were led by Paulo Fonseca in only a third game in charge since being prised from Lyon for roughly £4.5m compensation.

Five minutes after the break, United pulled ahead. First, a marauding Martínez was fouled by Eduardo Quaresma and Marciniak awarded a third penalty, which Bruno Fernandes converted for the first goal of the Pochettino era. Then, the captain scored a remarkable second.

A speculative left-foot shot from outside the area looked harmless before hitting a divot in front of Pereira, bouncing over the goalkeeper, and in. Fortune, at last, smiled on United and in replays it transpired Fernandes himself had accidentally created the divot just moments earlier.

On 65 minutes Pochettino made a move, as Dorgu and Diogo Dalot came on, Bryan Mbeumo becoming the centre-forward. United were a yard quicker, more streetwise: confidence and belief surging. On 77 minutes Diallo was forced off, Shea Lacey replacing him. But then came the latest chaos to engulf Pochettino’s nascent tenure.

items.lbText:
Mauricio Pochettino said after game it was ‘never a foul’

‘No one’s coming to save us,’ admits Kobbie Mainoo

Manchester United intend to appeal against the red card Leny Yoro received in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday. The defender was dismissed after fouling Alexander Isak outside the penalty area but Mauricio Pochettino believes the striker would not have reached the ball to take him through on goal against Senne Lammens and therefore it was not worthy of a sending-off .

United’s head coach said: “I don’t agree because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control. Leny was running with him and when Isak saw the control wasn’t good and the ball was going to the keeper it is normal you delay, you stop running, and you wait to feel the touch and you go down. It is never a foul.”

Dominik Szoboszlai scored from the resulting free-kick to give Liverpool the lead and Florian Wirtz doubled the lead three minutes later. Rio Ngumoha and Victor Muñoz completed the scoring as Pochettino lost his first game in charge of United, leaving them 19th in the Premier League.

“We’re at the lowest we’ve ever been and no one’s coming to save us,” the midfielder Kobbie Mainoo told MUTV. “There’s no helping hands coming so we’ve got to work together and lean on each other and keep working and hopefully it’ll come good.”

Yoro is due to serve a one-match ban at home to Brentford in the Premier League on Saturday. He is available for United’s Champions League match at Sporting on Wednesday.

items.title: Mauricio Pochettino can now see just how desperate Manchester United are | Jonathan Wilson
items.author: Jonathan Wilson
items.content:
The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided

In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter.

Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0. Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023. Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered.

items.title: Football Daily | Neville, Keane and Manchester United meltdowns at world’s funniest comedy club
items.author: Barry Glendenning
items.content:
Hoo-boy. Short of forgetting to put on his washable virgin wool navy trousers before striding towards the visitors’ dugout at Anfield, it’s difficult to imagine how Mauricio Pochettino’s spell in charge of Manchester United could have got off to a more humiliating start. Having witnessed his new team go a man and two goals down in less time than it takes to listen to Led Zeppelin’s Stairway to Heaven twice, it was a rendition of Sacked In The Morning that could be heard from the home fans inside 15 minutes. Poch would later complain that the decision to dismiss Leny Yoro was questionable, but it was far less baffling than his own call to hand Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in a year after almost 12 months out with knack. Across 90 harrowing minutes, the Dutch defender didn’t so much look off the pace as resemble a confused tourist who’d wandered on to the pitch while trying to find his way to the stadium museum.

In a footballing world obsessed with micro-marginal-gains – think custom-weighted laces, aerodynamic socks, or nice calming shades of green for training ground walls – how about one modest proposal that otherwise does my nut in? That a multimillion pound player, paid hundred of thousands each week, has to walk all the way around the pitch with ligament injuries. Carry him, give him crutches, or put him in a wheelchair! Is it just me? It has a very 1950s amateur air of ‘dont make a fuss, ‘tis a mere scratch’” – John Williams.

Since he was such a good friend to Mauricio Pochettino in his previous role, can we assume Donald Trump will be ringing the FA to overturn Lenny Yoro’s red card once he’s finished his morning nap?” – Declan Hackett.

Continue reading...

items.lbText:
Manchester United lose 4-0 to Liverpool after early red

Argentinian suffers club’s joint-heaviest debut defeat

Mauricio Pochettino argued that Leny Yoro was wrongly sent off and that Manchester United were earlier denied a penalty against Liverpool after suffering the joint-heaviest debut defeat in the club’s history.

Liverpool’s emphatic 4-0 win ensured Pochettino equalled Lal Hilditch’s unwanted record from 1926 of losing his first United game by such a scoreline. United’s 34 goals conceded across all competitions this season are the most by any team in European football’s top five leagues.

United were reduced to 10 men after only eight minutes when Yoro was shown a straight red card for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. “He was clearly the last man and it was clearly a foul,” said the Liverpool head coach, Andoni Iraola.

Yet Pochettino took a fiercely opposing view, claiming Isak had waited for contact to be made after losing possession and insisting United should have had a penalty moments earlier for a Jérémy Jacquet challenge on Bryan Mbeumo. Dominik Szoboszlai opened the scoring from the free-kick that resulted from Yoro’s foul and Liverpool were coasting at 2-0 after only 14 minutes. United’s head coach said: “I don’t agree [it was a red-card offence]because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control.

“Leny was running with him and when Isak saw the control wasn’t good and the ball was going to the keeper it is normal you delay, you stop running, and you wait to feel the touch and you go down. It is never a foul. But two minutes before, Jacquet and Mbeumo, how can you compare the situation?

“It is painful for me and for them but we played for more than 80 minutes at Anfield with 10 men. You can be critical of the team, but it’s a penalty for Mbeumo. We can make a mistake and we were punished. They can make a mistake and they were not punished.”

Pochettino defended his decision to give Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in 12 months despite the centre-back having a torrid time against Liverpool’s forward line. He also claimed United showed the resolve necessary to drag themselves out of relegation trouble despite being comprehensively outplayed.

“We need to accept the reality and we need to be united,” he said. “It is clear what happened.

“After eight minutes the plan was in the bin, but what I learned from my players is that they like to fight, they are committed to the team, to the club and they want to win games.

“Today was a test that for me is very positive. Even the best team in the world playing in these circumstances after eight minutes would concede four goals or even more. We are in a situation that is very complicated and difficult, but we fight, we make the effort.”

Rio Ngumoha became the youngest goalscorer in the fixture’s Premier League history and produced a scintillating display alongside the equally impressive Florian Wirtz. Iraola said of the teenager: “He is playing a lot of minutes, on the left and the right, and he is getting used to going outside or cutting inside to finish. I’m happy with the way he arrived in the box to score. The same with Flo. We want them to be more of a threat in the box.”

Iraola recreated Jürgen Klopp’s post-match celebration after the final whistle and fist-pumped the Kop. He said: “Obviously I enjoyed the moment. I still think we owe the fans because they have been very supportive and we’ve had much better results away from home than at home. This is a big game for everyone in the club and we wanted to give them a big win.”

This ended as a 4-0 rout in favour of Liverpool, the new head coach overseeing the poorest opening result of the eight who have followed Sir Alex Ferguson since May 2013. Factor in this result coming against United’s fiercest rivals and Pochettino’s despair is complete.

items.lbText:
Decision to pick the Dutch defender over Harry Maguire backfired as Manchester United fell apart in the Anfield bearpit

Chaotic, bewildering, and on this evidence in a relegation dogfight: welcome to the three‑ring circus that is Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino .

This ended as a 4-0 rout in favour of Liverpool, the new head coach overseeing the poorest opening result of the eight who have followed Sir Alex Ferguson since May 2013. Factor in this result coming against United’s fiercest rivals and Pochettino’s despair is complete.

He is firmly in the dock for this loss, due to a disastrous preference for Matthijs de Ligt over Harry Maguire, the hapless Dutch defender playing a leading part in three Liverpool goals.

Towards the end the Kop chirped: “You’re going down with the City.” There may be truth in the humour unless Pochettino gets hold – fast – of the rabble inherited from Michael Carrick .

Eight short minutes into a nascent tenure and a disgusted shake of his flowing locks was the greeting to the madhouse he has taken over. By then Leny Yoro had been sent off for bringing down Alexander Isak and Anfield was in bearpit mood.

Very far from ideal – and worse was to follow. Far worse. After the Frenchman departed, Dominik Szoboszlai smashed the free-kick through a nonexistent wall and beyond Senne Lammens and Liverpool were 1-0 up.

The visitors’ next act? To enter full meltdown as Diogo Dalot allowed Rio Ngumoha room to cross and Florian Wirtz hooked home, De Ligt losing his man.

Thirteen minutes in and 2–0 behind made Omar Berrada’s talk of the “buzz” of Pochettino’s entrance at United farcical and made the chief executive appear to be as much as a chump as his latest appointee, who was authoring a new head-coach plummet, not bounce.

Yoro had been forced into hauling down Isak after De Ligt lost first the ball, then the Liverpool striker. De Ligt’s inclusion was Pochettino’s headline selection move, the dropping of Maguire handing the centre-back a first league start in a year and it backfired almost immediately.

“I don’t know who played the last game – we assessed the squad from the day we arrived and we believe it’s the best team for today,” Pochettino said beforehand when quizzed about the XI he sent out.

Words to haunt him and, as De Ligt’s only other start was in United’s 4-1 humiliation at Como last month in the Champions League, questions regarding the coach’s judgment were already being posed.

By now “sacked in the morning” was the derisory cry of Kopites as Pochettino’s new project was in the damage-limitation mode of a 5-3-1 with 21 minutes played, as off went Bryan Mbeumo for Maguire.

After spells with Espanyol, Southampton, Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and the USA, Pochettino’s honours roll reads one Ligue 1 and one Coupe de France – a modest two trophies in a 17-year managerial career.

Losing a Champions League final (with Spurs) and two EFL Cup finals (Spurs and Chelsea) had characterised him, to some, as a “bridesmaid” and at half‑time his team were definitively second best, fortunate to be only two behind.

In the perpetual soap opera that is United, the buildup featured a drone filming Pochettino’s first training session, Berrada’s interview and Bruno Fernandes saying new contract talks between the captain and club were paused due to the worst league start in 40 years.

Going into the game, United’s dire form contained a solitary win in 10 league matches and eight points. Why? Because they are a rabble, lacking cohesion from goalkeeper to attack, with individuals consistently embarrassing themselves and the shirt.

It cost Carrick, culpable for this too, his job and cleared the path for Pochettino to occupy a role he has long coveted. Each new manager since Ferguson has faced a two-pronged challenge: the state of the squad and the state of the club – each related.

Those who know Pochettino say he will bring charm and warmth – useful, maybe, for man-managing a group of multimillionaires, but at the interval he needed to perform the miracle of convincing them that something, somehow, could be salvaged after a diabolical opening 45 minutes.

They were staring at defeat by an Andoni Iraola side that began 10 points and 15 places better off. Pochettino hoped to avoid this by taking off Matheus Cunha for Joshua Zirkzee for the second half but ended the non-contest ashen‑faced, with Berrada and Jason Wilcox, the director of football, appearing just as lost in the posh seats.

A main takeaway from Berrada’s interview was his conviction that “we are heading in the right direction”. When he spoke United were 18th, and by full time they were 19th, with De Ligt a glaring emblem of their disarray. When again he was marking air not Isak, the Swede saved the centre-back more blushes by spraying wide.

This had Pochettino applauding, unfathomably, when invective seemed an apt response.

Yet when Ngumoha made it 3-0 after 66 minutes there was no more faux touchline enthusiasm from a man who had promised to “create something from scratch”. As with all who have followed Ferguson, he had discovered that United’s shaky foundations make building anything sustainable a sisyphean task.

De Ligt’s loose pass led to Víctor Muñoz’s fourth, meaning the answer to whether Pochettino’s debut could have gone any worse was a resounding no.

items.lbText:
Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United . On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino endured a baptism of fire from the eighth minute onwards when Leny Yoro was sent off for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. Liverpool would not be denied anything else while tormenting their old rivals yet again.

Andoni Iraola indulged in his first fist-pumps towards the Kop after an utterly dominant, comfortable win illuminated by Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz brilliance plus goals from Dominik Szoboszlai and Víctor Muñoz. Liverpool’s two creative forces were also on the scoresheet as Ngumoha became the youngster scorer in the fixture’s Premier League history.

“Poch is at the wheel” was the mocking, merciless soundtrack that accompanied the end of the former Tottenham, Chelsea and USA coach’s first traumatic game in the job. There may well be more. On this evidence, 19th in the Premier League is not a misleading reflection of United’s position.

The latest calamity in United’s worst start to a season for 40 years cannot be pinned on a head coach who met his new charges only on Wednesday. There can be no genuine takes on Pochettino’s vision for United either, given how quickly he was forced to turn his first game into a damage-limitation exercise. But there was one firm conclusion to be drawn. His first big call in the job proved a serious mistake with destructive repercussions for United’s entire evening.

That ill-fated decision was to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 12 months at the expense of Harry Maguire. Maguire may be a symbol of United’s inertia, but his replacement at centre-back was heavily responsible for the chaos that quickly unfolded. The Netherlands international was at fault for three goals. Liverpool , under instruction from Iraola to start strong and “make them feel pressure from the beginning”, could hardly believe their luck at the first mishap in the visitors’ central defence.

De Ligt lost the flight of the ball and his man, Isak, when Ronald Araújo pinged a routine pass down Liverpool’s right-hand channel. Isak was suddenly away, De Ligt all at sea, and to compound matters Yoro was slow to react to the danger. By the time United’s covering defender was across to challenge Isak it was too late. Yoro clattered into the back of the Sweden international just outside the area and was shown a straight red card by the referee, Sam Barrott. Isak’s heavy first touch could not save Yoro. The free-kick could not save United from double jeopardy. Szoboszlai swept a powerful set piece into Senne Lammens’ bottom right-hand corner from 19 yards.

Pochettino claimed the dismissal was wrong and United should have had a penalty moments earlier for a Jérémy Jacquet challenge on Bryan Mbeumo. It was a desperate take. A simple detail showed the extent of the job United’s latest head coach has on his hands: the wall that lined up to face Szoboszlai’s free-kick. Just getting that right was beyond this group of players. White shirts lined up to protect the left side of Lammens’ goal but, with the isolated exception of Bruno Fernandes, no one covered the spot where the ball was ultimately placed.

Liverpool devoured the gifts. When the hosts doubled their lead three minutes later thoughts of another 7-0 humiliation for United did not seem unreasonable. Ngumoha tormented Diogo Dalot from the first whistle, as everyone inside the ground expected he would. Having been found by Isak’s cross-field pass the teenager breezed past Dalot to the byline and lifted a cross slightly behind Wirtz. The German playmaker, left in space by De Ligt, improvised brilliantly to hook a volley into the roof of the net while floating in mid-air. United were sinking into the abyss.

The first chants of “sacked in the morning” flowed from the Kop towards a disbelieving United head coach. There were 14 minutes on the clock. It was, of course, a ludicrous chant. It might be months before United’s hapless owners are seeking another scapegoat.

Pochettino responded in the only way he could to the onslaught and introduced Maguire into a rejigged five-man defence. Whether in the knowledge that United possessed neither the ability nor the inclination to hurt them, Liverpool eased off for the remainder of the first half although Isak and Alexis Mac Allister could have extended the lead.

Liverpool did not let their rivals off so lightly after the restart. Bradley Barcola could and should have provided Wirtz with a hat-trick of assists but squandered three beautiful touches from his fellow £100m+ recruit. Virgil van Dijk put a free header wide from another fine delivery by Wirtz. Barcola turned provider in devastating style, however, to create the goal Ngumoha’s display richly deserved. The France winger burst away from Lisandro Martínez and Fernandes with one flick of the ball before delivering an assist on a plate for the teenager to convert.

Iraola’s thoughts started to drift towards the midweek Champions League trip to Club Brugge and he started resting players from the 72nd minute onwards. But Liverpool were not done. Another mistake by De Ligt, this time a sloppy pass infield, was pounced on by Wirtz who released Muñoz inside the box. The Liverpool substitute stroked an emphatic finish past Lammens. All Sir Alex Ferguson could do up in the directors’ box in the closing stages was laugh with his friend the actor James Nesbit. The alternative is too bleak for a proud United man to contemplate.

items.lbText:
Bruno Fernandes has revealed that he put contract talks with Manchester United on hold after being offered a new deal.

Speaking to Sky Sports ahead of the match against Liverpool, the United captain explained: “No, there’s no negotiations ongoing, but I’ve seen people saying that he’s asked for more money, he’s asked for more years. If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here. I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.

“Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here. The thing is, I’ve always showed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club. And I always said, in the moment the club thinks it’s time for me to move on, I will move on.

“I’m not going to be the player that I’ve seen many in this time at Manchester United. They’re going to stay here just by staying, just finish my contract and then we will see. In the moment the club says, ‘Bruno, it’s time to part ways’, I’m going to be the first one walking out the door.

“Yeah, the club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay. And as you said, there are no negotiations going on.

“We spoke about the contract at the end of last season, we came in the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations because the most important thing now is that the club gets back to win games.”

Fernandes’ current deal expires at the end of the season, but Manchester United have the option to extend it by another year.
